nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:L}\Cref{thm:main} should be compared with the trivial bound $S_1 \ll V_1\cdots V_{J} N$. 

We stated \cref{thm:main} with the constant $3/4$ in \cref{eq:summainthm}, but our proof works for any exponent $>2/3$. In principle, this exponent could be improved to $1/2+o(1)$. However, a proof of this would involve combinatorial complications and would not significantly improve the constant~$c$ in \cref{cor:manipulation} (which is unspecified anyway).

The lower bound for $N$ in terms of $H$ can be somewhat relaxed, but the proof definitely requires something like $\log N \geqslant (\log H)^{2+o(1)}$.

\label{lem:primesets}
Let $\varepsilon_1>0$ be a sufficiently small constant. Let $H>0$ be sufficiently large in terms of $\varepsilon_1$. Let $1\leqslant J \leqslant \varepsilon_1^2 \log \log H$, and let $H_0 = \exp \big((\log H)^{1-\varepsilon_1}\big)$.

Let $\mathcal{P}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{P}_{J}$ be as in \cref{thm:main}. Let $V_i := \sum_{p\in \mathcal{P}_i} \frac 1p$ and define $V := \max_{i\in \sinterval{J}} V_i$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=\alph*]
	\item \label{item:primesetsm1} $\mathcal{P}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{P}_{J}$ are disjoint subsets of $(H_0, H)$,
	\item \label{item:primesets7} $V_1V_2\cdots V_{J} = (1+o(1))V^{J} = (1+o(1)) \left(\displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon_1 \log \log H}{2J}\right)^{J}$,
	\item \label{item:primesets8} if $(p_1, \ldots, p_{J}) \in \mathcal{P}_1\times \cdots \times \mathcal{P}_{J}$, then $p_1p_2\cdots p_i < p_{i+1}^{1/10}$ for all $1\leqslant i <J$, and $p_1p_2\cdots p_{J}<H$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $V^{J} \ll (\log H)^{\varepsilon_1^2 \log (\varepsilon_1^{-1})}$. If, moreover, $J \geqslant \frac{\varepsilon_1^2}{2} \log \log H$, then $V^{J} \gg (\log H)^{\frac{\varepsilon_1^2}{2} \log (\varepsilon_1^{-1})}$.

nodes.name: Two-point Chowla at almost all scales
nodes.statement: Our main result also implies an improved quantitative version of Chowla's conjecture for two-point correlations at almost all scales. Namely, for all e<wleqslant X, we have frac1log w int_X/w^X absfrac1x sum_nleqslant x lambda(n) lambda(n+1) fracdxx ll frac1(log w)^c, where c>0 is an absolute constant. This almost all scales result crefeq:almostallscales follows from crefeq:summainthmABSVAL by a straightforward adaptation of the proof in (which is itself inspired from ) to our setting.

Any $\boldsymbol{d}\in \mathbf{D}_{\!K}$ induces a partition of $\sinterval{K}\times\sinterval{J}$, where $(i,j)$ and $(i',j')$ are in the same class if and only if $\pcomp{i}{j} = \pcomp{i'}{j'}$. Every class $\alpha$ of the partition is contained in $\sinterval{K}\times \{j_{\alpha}\}$ for some $j_{\alpha}\in \sinterval{J}$, because the sets $\mathcal{P}_j$ are disjoint. Observe that $\boldsymbol{d}$ is fully determined by a sequence of $K$ signs (the signs of the $d_i$), such a partition of $\sinterval{K}\times\sinterval{J}$ and the assignment of a prime in $\mathcal{P}_{\! j_{\alpha}}$ to every class $\alpha$ of this partition (the prime factors of the $d_i$). 

Summing over all sequences of signs $\sigma$, suitable partitions $\Pi$ of $\sinterval{K}\times\sinterval{J}$ and primes in $\mathcal{P}$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\boldsymbol{d}\in \mathbf{D}_{\!K}} \, \prod_{p\mid \fprod{\boldsymbol{d}}} \frac{1}{p} \leqslant  \sum_{\sigma\in \{\pm1\}^{K}} \sum_{\Pi} \,\prod_{\alpha\in \Pi} \,\sum_{p_{\alpha}\in \mathcal{P}_{\!j_{\alpha}}} \frac{1}{p_{\alpha}} \leqslant 2^{K} (K J)^{K J} V^{K J},
\end{equation*}
where we used that the number of partitions of $\sinterval{K}\times\sinterval{J}$ is $\leqslant (K J)^{K J}$.

\begin{itemize}
	\item $\pcomp{i}{j}\mid n+b_i$ for all $(i,j)\in \mathcal{L}$,
	\item and $\omega_{\mathcal{P}}(n+b_i)\leqslant 2JV$ for all $i\in \sinterval{R}$.

Suppose first that there are two indices $(i,j), (i', j)\in \mathcal{L}$ such that $\pcomp{i}{j} = \pcomp{i'}{j}$. Since $(i,j), (i', j)\in \mathcal{L}$ we have $\pcomp{i}{j} \mid n+b_i$ and $\pcomp{i}{j} = \pcomp{i'}{j} \mid n+b_{i'}$, and thus $\pcomp{i}{j} \mid b_i - b_{i'}$. Hence \cref{item:litcond1} is satisfied.

Let $k\in \sinterval{R}$. On the one hand, for all $(i,j)\in \mathcal{L}$, having $\pcomp{i}{j}\mid b_i-b_k$ implies that $\pcomp{i}{j} \mid n+b_k$, because we also know that $\pcomp{i}{j}\mid n+b_i$ as $(i,j)\in \mathcal{L}$. On the other hand, by assumption we know that $n+b_k$ has at most $2JV$ prime factors in $\mathcal{P}$. We denote the set of all positions of the letter uplettersA in w by poswuplettersA := \kin sintervaln : w[k] = uplettersA\. For lin sintervaln, we also write posbiswl := \kin sintervaln : w[k] = w[l]\ (instead of `posbisww[l]'). \label{def:words}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set (the alphabet). Let $\mathcal{W}_n$ be the set of all $n$-letter words on $\mathcal{A}$, where no two consecutive letters are the same. Let $\mathcal{W}_n^{\neq} \subset \mathcal{W}_n$ be the set of all $n$-letter words on $\mathcal{A}$ with distinct letters. Let $\mathcal{W} = \bigcup_{n\geqslant 1}\mathcal{W}_n$ and $\mathcal{W}^{\neq} = \bigcup_{n\geqslant 1}\mathcal{W}_n^{\neq}$.

For $w\in \mathcal{W}_n$ and $1\leqslant k\leqslant n$, we write $w[k]$ for the $k$-th letter of $w$. We denote by $\letters{w}$ the set of all letters of $w$.

We denote the set of all positions of the letter \upletters{A} in $w$ by $\pos{w}{\upletters{A}} := \{k\in \sinterval{n} : w[k] = \upletters{A}\}$. For $l\in \sinterval{n}$, we also write $\posbis{w}{l} :=  \{k\in \sinterval{n} : w[k] = w[l]\}$ (instead of `$\posbis{w}{w[l]}$').

The notation $v \sqsubset w$ means that $v$ is a \emph{substring} of $w$, i.e.~a sequence of consecutive letters of $w$. 

We write $\overline{w}$ for the word obtained by writing the letters of $w$ in the reversed order. 

The \emph{concatenation} of two words $w_1$ and $w_2$ is the word obtained by appending the letters of $w_2$ at the end of $w_1$. We denote it by $w_1w_2$.

nodes.statement: A prime pin P is said to be involved in a constraint `pcompi_0j_0 mid sum_iin I d_i + z' if (at least) one of the following holds: [label=(roman*), ref=roman*] item z=0, sum_iin I d_i = 0 and sum_substackiin I\\ p mid d_i d_i neq 0, or item z=0, p = pcompi_0j_0 and sum_substackiin I\\ p nmid d_i d_i neq 0, or item p neq pcompi_0j_0 and sum_substackiin I\\ p mid d_i d_i notequiv 0 pmodpcompi_0j_0. If case crefitem:const1 holds, we will say that p is crefitem:const1-involved in the corresponding constraint. We similarly define crefitem:const2-involved and crefitem:const3-involved primes.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:involved}
A prime $p\in \mathcal{P}$ is said to be \emph{involved} in a constraint `$\pcomp{i_0}{j_0} \mid \sum_{i\in I} d_i + z$' if (at least) one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=\roman*]
	\item \label{item:const1} $z=0$, $\displaystyle{\sum_{i\in I} d_i = 0}$ and $\displaystyle{\sum_{\substack{i\in I\\ p \mid d_i}} d_i \neq 0}$, or
	\item \label{item:const2} $z=0$, $p = \pcomp{i_0}{j_0}$ and $\displaystyle{\sum_{\substack{i\in I\\ p \nmid d_i}} d_i \neq 0}$, or
	\item \label{item:const3} $p \neq \pcomp{i_0}{j_0}$ and $\displaystyle{\sum_{\substack{i\in I\\ p \mid d_i}} d_i \not\equiv 0 \pmod{\pcomp{i_0}{j_0}}}$.
\end{enumerate}
If case \cref{item:const1} holds, we will say that $p$ is \cref{item:const1}-involved in the corresponding constraint. We similarly define \cref{item:const2}-involved and \cref{item:const3}-involved primes.

nodes.raw_latex:
Let $J_1$ be the set of all $j\in \sinterval{4m}$ such that $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$ contains a letter not appearing in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$. Similarly, let $J_2$ be the set of all $j\in \sinterval{4m}$ such that $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$ has a letter that is not present in $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$. By assumption, $J_1 \cup J_2 = \sinterval{4m}$, so one of $J_1$ and $J_2$ has size $\geqslant 2m$. Without loss of generality, assume that $\abs{J_1} \geqslant 2m$, swapping $w_1$ and $w_2$ if necessary.

Let $j\in J_1$, and let $\upletters{X}$ be a letter present in $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$ but not in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$. The letter \upletters{X} could possibly appear in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{0}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}}}$ or in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j}\ldots Y\makesubscript{4m}}}$, but not in both as $w_2 \in \mathcal{W}^{\neq}$.

We define $J_1^<$ to be the set of all $j\in J_1$ for which there exists a letter $\upletters{X}$ present in $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$ but not in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{0}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$. Similarly, we define $J_1^>$ to be the set of all $j\in J_1$ for which there exists a letter $\upletters{X}$ of $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j}}}$ not appearing in $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{4m}}}$. By the previous observation, we have $J_1^<\cup J_1^> = J_1$, so one of $J_1^<$ and $J_1^>$ has size $\geqslant m$. Considering the reversed words if necessary, we may assume without loss of generality that $\abs{J_1^<} \geqslant m$.

Let $j_1<j_2<\ldots<j_m$ be elements of $J_1^<$. For $i\in \sinterval{m}$, let $\upletters{X\makesubscript{i}}$ be a letter of $w_1|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{j_i\!-\!1}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j_i}}}$ not appearing in the substring $w_2|_{\upletters{Y\makesubscript{0}\ldots Y\makesubscript{j_i}}}$ of $w_2$. nodes.statement: Define a strict partial order prec^1 on S by setting (a,b) prec^1 (c,d) iff b<c. A well-known consequence of Dilworth's theorem states that any partially ordered set on n elements contains a chain or an antichainfootnoteRecall that a chain is a totally ordered subset of a partially ordered set, and an antichain is a subset in which no two elements are comparable. of size geqslant n^1/2 (see ). If S contains a chain of size geqslant n^1/2 for prec^1, we are in case crefitem:pairs1. Suppose that S contains an antichain A of size geqslant n^1/2. We introduce another partial order prec^2 on A by defining (a,b) prec^2 (c,d) iff a<c<d<b. By the same combinatorial fact, either A contains a chain for prec^2 of size geqslant n^1/4, and case crefitem:pairs3 applies, or A contains an antichain A' for prec^2 of size geqslant n^1/4. Suppose that the latter possibility occurs. Let (a_1, b_1), ldots, (a_n', b_n') be the elements of A', with a_1<a_2 <cdots < a_n'. Since A' is an antichain for prec^1, all the b_i are greater than a_n'. Since A' is also an antichain for prec^2, we deduce that b_1<b_2<cdots <b_n', and we are in case~crefitem:pairs2.
nodes.raw_latex: Define a strict partial order $\prec^1$ on $S$ by setting $(a,b) \prec^1 (c,d)$ iff $b<c$. A well-known consequence of Dilworth's theorem states that any partially ordered set on $n$ elements contains a chain or an antichain\footnote{Recall that a \emph{chain} is a totally ordered subset of a partially ordered set, and an \emph{antichain} is a subset in which no two elements are comparable.} of size $\geqslant n^{1/2}$ (see \cite[Proposition~2.5.9]{ordered}). If $S$ contains a chain of size $\geqslant n^{1/2}$ for $\prec^1$, we are in case \cref{item:pairs1}. Suppose that $S$ contains an antichain $A$ of size $\geqslant n^{1/2}$. We introduce another partial order $\prec^2$ on $A$ by defining $(a,b) \prec^2 (c,d)$ iff $a<c<d<b$. By the same combinatorial fact, either $A$ contains a chain for $\prec^2$ of size $\geqslant n^{1/4}$, and case \cref{item:pairs3} applies, or $A$ contains an antichain $A'$ for $\prec^2$ of size $\geqslant n^{1/4}$. Suppose that the latter possibility occurs. Let $(a_1, b_1), \ldots, (a_{n'}, b_{n'})$ be the elements of $A'$, with $a_1<a_2 <\cdots < a_{n'}$. Since $A'$ is an antichain for $\prec^1$, all the $b_i$ are greater than $a_{n'}$. Since $A'$ is also an antichain for $\prec^2$, we deduce that $b_1<b_2<\cdots <b_{n'}$, and we are in case~\cref{item:pairs2}.

nodes.statement: By definition of unpredictability, either w contains a letter repeated >t times, or it has >t letters with variable neighbours. In the first case, we immediately see that w has lfloor t/2 rfloor repetitions. This is geqslant t^c_1 if c_1 is sufficiently small. Suppose now that there are >t letters with variable neighbours in w. Let E be the set of all these letters, with the possible exception of the first and last letters of w which are discarded (to simplify the notation below). Thus, absE geqslant t-2. For every letter uplettersA in E, there are two positions 1<k_uplettersA<l_uplettersA<n such that w[k_uplettersA] = w[l_uplettersA] = uplettersA, and the sets of letters adjacent to these two occurrences of uplettersA are different, i.e.~\w[k_uplettersA-1], w[k_uplettersA+1]\ neq \w[l_uplettersA-1], w[l_uplettersA+1]\. We apply creflem:combipairs to the set S = \(k_uplettersA, l_uplettersA) : uplettersAin E\. If case crefitem:pairs1 occurs, we can immediately conclude that w has gg t^1/4 separated repetitions and we are done. Suppose that case crefitem:pairs2 of creflem:combipairs applies. This implies that, for some cgg1, there exists a subset F = \uplettersAmakesubscript1,ldots,uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF\subset E of size absF geqslant t^c such that 1<k_uplettersAmakesubscript1<k_uplettersAmakesubscript2<cdots <k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF<l_uplettersAmakesubscript1<l_uplettersAmakesubscript2<cdots <l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF<n. By creflem:unpredstep0, either w has gg t^c/2 separated repetitions, and the first conclusion holds, or we can find a `large' substring of w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF] with distinct letters. Without loss of generality (by replacing F with a smaller subset, c with a smaller absolute constant and relabelling the letters), we may thus assume that the word w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF] itself has distinct letters. By a further application of creflem:unpredstep0, we may also assume that the word w[l_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[l_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF] has distinct letters. We apply creflem:unpredstep4 with w_1 := w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF] and w_2 := w[l_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[l_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF]. These are two words in W^neq of the form uplettersAmakesubscript1ldots Amakesubscript2ldots Amakesubscript3ldots cdots uplettersldots AmakesubscriptabsF, so the assumptions of creflem:unpredstep4 are satisfied (of course, we may assume that absF equiv 1 pmod8 without loss of generality). The conclusion of creflem:unpredstep4 provides us with two words v_1 and v_2 precisely satisfying the second conclusion of crefprop:structureunpred. The treatment of case crefitem:pairs3 of creflem:combipairs is similar. For some cgg1, there exists a subset F = \uplettersAmakesubscript1,ldots,uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF\subset E of size absF geqslant t^c such that 1<k_uplettersAmakesubscript1<k_uplettersAmakesubscript2<cdots <k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF<l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF<l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF\!-\!1<cdots <l_uplettersAmakesubscript1<n. By two successive applications creflem:unpredstep0, we may assume, without loss of generality, that the substrings w_1 := w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1]w[k_uplettersAmakesubscript1+1]cdots w[k_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF] and w_2 := w[l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF]w[l_uplettersAmakesubscriptabsF-1]cdots w[l_uplettersAmakesubscript1] each have distinct letters. Then, applying creflem:unpredstep4 with these two substrings w_1 and w_2 produces two words v_1 and v_2 with the required properties.

Let c_1>0 be the constant in the statement of crefprop:structureunpred. We can safely assume that K^c_1/8 geqslant 400K^10varepsilon_1 since c_1 is a fixed absolute constant (that could in principle be computed) and varepsilon_1 is assumed to be sufficiently small. By crefprop:structureunpred, one the following holds. item The first possibility is that w_j,boldsymbold has geqslant K^c_1/4 separated repetitions. By creflem:seprepstep2, boldsymbold satisfies a triangular system of complexity (lceil K^c_1/4/100 rceil ;1,0). item Otherwise, the second conclusion of crefprop:structureunpred holds with mgeqslant K^c_1/4, which means that the hypotheses of creflem:seprepstep3 are satisfied, and hence the concatenation of boldsymbold and -boldsymbold satisfies a triangular system of constraints of complexity (lceil K^c_1/4/(200K^10varepsilon_1)rceil ;2,K H). In either case, the concatenation of boldsymbold and -boldsymbold satisfies a triangular system of constraints of complexity (lceil 2K^c_1/8 rceil ;2,K H). Note that K H K^22R J ll K^O(K J) as Hleqslant e^K and Rleqslant K. Moreover, since log H_0 gg K^1-varepsilon_1 and c_1geqslant 80varepsilon_1 we have H_0^-K^c_1/8 ll expbig(-K^1+c_1/16big). We need to count the number of possibilities for pcompRj, given that it should be of the form pcompRj = pcompij for some iin sintervalR-2 with (i,j)in L. Since boldsymbold has to satisfy property crefitem:litcond1 of creflem:litcond, we know that pcompRj must be an element of the set A_j := \pcompij \, :\, iin sintervalR-2, \, (i,j)in L, \, pcompij mid b_R-1 - b_i\ (recalling that pcompRj = pcomp(R-1)j, and thus b_R-1 = sum_k<R-1 d_k equiv b_Rpmod pcompRj). Let us make a preliminary observation. For 0leqslant m_1 < m_2leqslant M, the composition iota_m_2^-1 circ iota_m_1 : sintervalK_m_1 to sintervalK_m_2 is well-defined, injective, and its image is contained in sintervalK_m_2-2 since the last two entries of boldsymbold^(m_2) correspond to a new backtracking pair. nodes.statement: The weighted graph G introduced in crefdef:Gamma satisfies the first two properties of crefprop:smalltrace: the first one by creflem:introducingcutoff, and the second by construction. We then sum over all possibilities boldsymbold' for the reduced walk given this data, and finally over all boldsymbold with reduced walk widetildeboldsymbold = boldsymbold'. Suppose first that there are $\geqslant \tfrac13K^{1/2}$ indices $(i, j)\in \mathcal{S}$ for which there exists $(i',j')\in \mathcal{S}$ with $b_i = b_{i'}$ and $i\neq i'$. We use the pigeonhole principle on the second coordinate $j$. We see that, for some $j_0\in \sinterval{J}$, there is a set $\mathcal{I}$ of $\geqslant \tfrac16 K^{1/2}/J$ elements $i\in \sinterval{K}$ with the above properties, i.e.~$(i,j_0)\in \mathcal{S}$ and there exists $(i',j')\in \mathcal{S}$ with $b_i = b_{i'}$ and $i<i'$. In particular, for any $i\in \mathcal{I}$, there is some $i'>i$ such that
\begin{equation*}
	\pcomp{K}{1} \ \Big\vert\  0 = b_{i'} - b_i = \sum_{i\leqslant k<i'} d_k,
\end{equation*}

For any $i\in \mathcal{I}$, we choose such an $i'$ (arbitrarily) and denote by $C_i$ the resulting constraint $C_{\interval{i}{i'-1},K,1,0}(\boldsymbol{d})$. Note that the prime $\pcomp{i}{j_0}$ is {\cref{item:const1}-involved} in $C_i$, since we have ${\sum_{i\leqslant k<i',\,\pcomp{i}{j_0}\mid d_k}d_k = d_i \neq 0}$ as $(i,j_0)\in \mathcal{S}$. Moreover, for any $i_1,i_2\in \mathcal{I}$ with $i_1<i_2$, the prime $\pcomp{i_1}{j_0}$ is absent from $C_{i_2}$. Therefore, the sequence $(C_i)_{i\in \mathcal{I}}$ (in decreasing order of $i\in \mathcal{I}$) forms a triangular system of constraints satisfied by $\boldsymbol{d}$, of complexity $(\lfloor \tfrac16 K^{1/2}/J\rfloor; 1, 0)$.

Case \cref{item:bad2} of \cref{def:badsingle} is treated in an analogous way. Suppose there are $\geqslant \tfrac13K^{1/2}$ indices $(i, j)\in \mathcal{S}$ for which there exists $(i',j')\in \mathcal{S}$ with $b_{i+1} = b_{i'+1}$ and $i\neq i'$. \begin{equation*}
	\pcomp{i}{j_0} \ \Big\vert\ b_{i} - b_{i'} = \sum_{i'\leqslant k<i} d_k \neq 0.
\end{equation*}
For every $i\in \mathcal{I}$, we choose an appropriate $i'$ and denote by $C_i$ the constraint $C_{\interval{i'}{i-1},i,j_0,0}(\boldsymbol{d})$. The prime $\pcomp{i}{j_0}$ is \cref{item:const2}-involved in $C_i$, as $(i,j_0)\in \mathcal{S}$. nodes.statement: Let X be the set of all R_1in (Y-boldsymbolb)^cap of the form R_1 = Rcap A_boldsymbold for some Rin Y_T. Since the prime factors of q_A_boldsymbold are in P', we may rewrite sum_substackRin Y_T prod_substackpmid q_R\\ pnotin P' frac1p = sum_R_1in X prod_substackpmid q_R_1\\ pnotin P'frac1p sum_substackRin Y_T\\ Rcap A_boldsymbold = R_1 1. To bound the inner sum, we use the following fact: for any arithmetic progression R_1 and any dmid q_R_1, there is a unique arithmetic progression Rsupset R_1 with q_R_1/q_R = d, and moreover all progressions Rsupset R_1 are obtained in this way. Therefore, the inner sum is bounded by the number of divisors of q_R_1. For every R_1in X, we have omega(q_R_1) ll KJ. This follows from crefeq:expressionR1 as in the proof of part crefitem:rank2 of creflem:existencerank. Therefore, q_R_1 has e^O(KJ) divisors, and hence the inner sum is e^O(KJ). It remains to show that sum_R_1in X prod_substackpmid q_R_1\\ pnotin P'frac1p ll e^O(KJ). This is a simple counting problem, similar to creflem:trivialbound or crefprop:predictablevector. However, the notation is much heavier in this case. Let R_1in X. By definition of Y_T and X, we can write R_1 = bigcap_tin sintervalT big(Q_t - b_k_tbig) cap A_boldsymbold for some Q_tin Y and some k_tin sintervalK. For tin sintervalT, let boldsymbold^(t) be a primitive prohibited sequence having Q_t as its associated prohibited progression. Let ell_t be the length of boldsymbold^(t) and let sigma_tin \pm1\^ell_t be the sequence of signs of the coordinates of boldsymbold^(t). As usual, for (i,j)in sintervalell_t \!times \!sintervalJ we write d^(t)_ij for the unique prime in P_j dividing d^(t)_i. Let sim be the equivalence relation on bigsqcup_tin sintervalT big(\t\\!times \!sintervalell_t \!times \!sintervalJbig) defined by (t_1,i_1,j_1) sim (t_2,i_2,j_2) iff d^(t_1)_i_1j_1 = d^(t_2)_i_2j_2. If alpha is an equivalence class for sim, we write p_alpha for the prime d^(t)_ij, where (t,i,j) is any element of~alpha. This definition does not depend on the choice of representative, by definition of sim. Let E be the set of all equivalence classes alpha for sim such that p_alpha in P'. Let phi : E toP' be the map defined by phi(alpha) = p_alpha. We call the tuple ((k_t)_tin sintervalT, (ell_t)_tin sintervalT, (sigma_t)_tin sintervalT, sim, E, phi) a template for R_1. Thus, to every progression R_1in X we may associate a template (note that there may not be a canonical choice for the template associated to R_1, as it depends on the choice of a representation of R_1 as in~crefeq:reprR1). Let Theta be the set of all tuples ((k_t)_tin sintervalT, (ell_t)_tin sintervalT, (sigma_t)_tin sintervalT, sim, E, phi) which are a template of some element R_1 in X. Fix some theta = ((k_t)_tin sintervalT, (ell_t)_tin sintervalT, (sigma_t)_tin sintervalT, sim, E, phi) in Theta. Let X_theta be the set of all R_1in X for which theta is a template. Suppose that X_theta is non-empty. Any R_1in X_theta is uniquely determined by the sequence of primes (p_alpha)_alphain E', where E' is the set of all equivalence classes of sim not in E. Thus sum_R_1in X_theta prod_substackpmid q_R_1\\ pnotin P'frac1p leqslant sum_(p_alpha)_alphain E' prod_alphain E' frac1p_alpha leqslant V^absE' leqslant V^T L J leqslant e^O(KJ), where we used that T ll K^5varepsilon_1 and L<K^1-10varepsilon_1 in the last inequality. We proceed to sum crefeq:partrank4bis over all choices of thetain Theta. We will be done provided that the number of possible templates is e^O(KJ). The number of choices for (k_t)_tin sintervalT, (ell_t)_tin sintervalT and (sigma_t)_tin sintervalT is at most K^T, L^T and (2^L)^T respectively. Since sim is an equivalence relation on a set of size leqslant T L J, there are leqslant (T L J)^T L J choices for sim. There are leqslant 2^T L J choices for E. Finally, phi is a map from a set of size leqslant T L J to a set of size leqslant 2 KJ, so there are leqslant (2KJ)^T L J possibilities for phi. For every tin sintervalT, let Gamma_t be the set of all constraints satisfied by boldsymbold^(t) of the form C_I,i_0,j_0,0(boldsymbold) for some discrete interval Isubset sintervalnellpt and some (i_0,j_0)in sintervalnellpt \!times\! sintervalJ, where nellpt is the length of boldsymbold^(t). Suppose first that there is a set Isubset sintervalT of size geqslant tfrac116 T such that, for every tin I, there is a constraint C_tin Gamma_t and a prime p_t which is involved in C_t and does not divide prod_s<tq_Q_s. Then, clearly, p_t is absent from C_s, for every sin I with s<t, which means that the constraints (C_t)_tin I form a triangular system of complexity (lfloor tfrac116 Trfloor; 1, 0). The same conclusion holds if there is a set Isubset sintervalT of size geqslant tfrac116 T such that, for every tin I, there is a constraint C_tin Gamma_t and a prime p_t which is involved in C_t and does not divide prod_s>tq_Q_s. We may thus assume that, for geqslant tfrac78 T values of tin sintervalT, every prime involved in some constraint of Gamma_t divides both prod_s<tq_Q_s and prod_s>tq_Q_s. nodes.statement: Observe that, given two finite sets Omega_1subset Omega_2, we have (-1)^|Omega_1| sum_Omega_1 subset W subset Omega_2 (-1)^|W| = indOmega_1=Omega_2. Indeed, this is obvious if Omega_1 = Omega_2, and if Omega_1neq Omega_2 the left-hand side is the expanded form of (1-1)^|Omega_2setminus Omega_1|. This allows us to write abssum_substackB subset A\\ cup B = Omega (-1)^|B| = abssum_B subset A (-1)^|B| sum_cup B subset W subset Omega (-1)^|W| = abssum_Wsubset Omega (-1)^|W| sum_substackB subset A\\ cup B subset W (-1)^|B| . The inner sum has the shape of crefeq:trickforcancellation, with Omega_1 = emptyset and Omega_2 = \Ain A mid Asubset W\, so is at most 1 in absolute value. Since the outer sum has leqslant 2^|Omega| terms, the claim follows.

nodes.statement: Let Y be a finite set of arithmetic progressions in Z with square-free moduli. Let Y^cap := \cap S : S subset Y\. Fix a non-empty subset X subset Y^cap that is closed under containment, i.e.~if a progression Pin Y^cap is an element of X, then so are all P'in Y^cap with P' supset P. Let X be the collection of subsets of Y defined byfootnoteNote that emptyset in X since cap emptyset = Z by convention. X = \S subset Y: cap S in X\. Then indnnotin P\ forall Pin Y = sum_Sin X (-1)^|S| indn in cap S + O left(sum_Rin partial X 3^omega(q_R) indnin Rright) where partial X := \Rin Y^cap: Rnotin X and R = Pcap P' for some Pin X and P'in Y \. Moreover, the first sum can be rewritten as sum_Sin X (-1)^|S| indn in cap S = sum_Pin X c_P indnin P for some coefficients c_Pin Z satisfying |c_P| leqslant 2^omega(q_P).

nodes.statement: If the left-hand side of crefeq:bonferronilike is 1, then the equality crefeq:bonferronilike is true by creflem:sieveidentity. On the other hand, if the left-hand side is 0, then by creflem:sieveidentity we have indnnotin P\ forall Pin Y = sum_Sin X (-1)^|S| indn in cap S + sum_substackP_0in S subset Y\\ S notin X,\, Ssetminus \P_0\ in X (-1)^|S| indnin cap S, where, in the last sum, P_0 in Y is an arbitrary progression containing n. We will bound the second sum at the end of this proof. Let us analyse the first sum. We have sum_Sin X (-1)^|S| indn in cap S = sum_Pin X c_P indnin P where, for Pin X , c_P := sum_substackSin X\\ cap S = P (-1)^|S| = sum_substackSsubset \P'in Y : P'supset P\ \\ cap S = P (-1)^|S|. Fix some Pin X. If S is a set of progressions containing P, the condition cap S = P is equivalent to lcm \q_P' : P'in S\ = q_P. Since all progressions in Y have square-free moduli, this is in turn equivalent to bigcup_P'in S \p : pmid q_P'\ = \p : pmid q_P\. Let Omega_P := \p : pmid q_P\, A_P := Big\ \p : pmid q_P'\ : P'in Y, P'supset PBig\ and, for every set S of progressions containing P, let B_P(S) := Big\ \p : pmid q_P'\ : P'in SBig\. Note that B_P(S) determines S, since a progression P'in Y with P'supset P is uniquely determined by its modulus q_P', which in turn is uniquely determined by its set of prime factors. Therefore, c_P = sum_substackSsubset \P'in Y : P'supset P\ \\ cap S = P (-1)^|S| = sum_substackB subset A_P \\ cup B = Omega_P (-1)^|B|. By creflem:rota, we obtain |c_P| leqslant 2^|Omega_P| = 2^omega(q_P). We now turn to the remainder term. We suppose that nin P_0 for some P_0in Y. We operate a change of variables and write S' = S setminus \P_0\, P = cap S' and R = cap S. The conditions S notin X and Ssetminus \P_0\ in X become Rnotin X and Pin X, respectively. Hence, we have sum_substackP_0in S subset Y\\ S notin X,\, Ssetminus \P_0\ in X (-1)^|S| indnin cap S = sum_substackRin Y^cap \\ Rnot in X indnin R sum_substackPin X \\ R = Pcap P_0sum_substackS'in X\\ cap S'= P (-1)^|S'|+1. The inner sum is exactly -c_P, which is Obig(2^omega(q_P)big). Recalling that, for fixed R, a progression Psupset R is uniquely determined by its modulus q_P, which divides q_R, we have sum_substackP_0in S subset Y\\ S notin X,\, Ssetminus \P_0\ in X (-1)^|S| indnin cap S = O left(sum_Rin partial X indnin R sum_dmid q_R 2^omega(d)right). The observation that sum_dmid m 2^omega(d) = 3^omega(m) for all square-free mgeqslant 1 concludes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let V_[M] :=sum_substackdin D_Icap (M/2, M]1/d. It suffices to show that T_M := sum_nin I_N sum_substackdin D_I\\ din (M/2, M]frac1d lambda(n) lambda(n+d) ll left(fracV^Jlog M+V_[M]right) fracN(log H)^1/1750 holds for all Min [H_0, H]. Indeed, summing this inequality for Min \H2^-j : jgeqslant 0\cap [H_0, H] gives the desired upper bound sum_nin I_N sum_substackdin D_Ifrac1d lambda(n) lambda(n+d) ll Big(V^J(log log H)+V^J Big) fracN(log H)^1/1750 ll fracV^J N(log H)^1/2000. To prove crefeq:dyadicsufficient, we start by introducing a new average over shifts mleqslant M and use the circle method: T_M &= frac1M sum_mleqslant M sum_nin I_N sum_substackdin D_I\\ din (M/2, M]frac1d lambda(n+m) lambda(n+m+d) + O(MV^J)\\ &= frac1M sum_nin I_N int_0^1 Q(alpha) F_n(alpha) G_n(alpha) dalpha + O(MV^J), with F_n(alpha):=sum_mleqslant Mlambda(n+m)e(alpha m), G_n(alpha):=sum_kleqslant 2Mlambda(n+k)e(-alpha k) and Q(alpha) as in creflem:fourthmoment. The error term O(MV^J) is clearly negligible. Let varepsilon>0 be a parameter that will be fixed later, and let E_varepsilon := \alphain [0, 1] : |Q(alpha)| > varepsilon\. Outside of E_varepsilon, the function |Q| is small and we have sum_nin I_N int_[0, 1]setminus E_varepsilon |Q||F_n| |G_n| leqslant varepsilon N normF_n_2 normG_n_2 ll varepsilon M N. On the other hand, the Lebesgue measure of E_varepsilon is ll curlyLexp4J/(varepsilon^4 M (log M)^4) by creflem:fourthmoment and Markov's inequality. Hence sum_nin I_N int_E_varepsilon |Q||F_n| |G_n| ll fraccurlyLexp4J normQ_infty varepsilon^4 M (log M)^4 normsum_nin I_N |F_n||G_n|_infty\!\! ll fraccurlyLexp4J \, V_[M]varepsilon^4 M (log M)^4 M normsum_nin I_N |F_n|_infty. We now make crucial use of to obtain normsum_nin I_N |F_n|_infty \!\! = sup_alphain R\, sum_nin I_N abssum_nleqslant n'leqslant n+M lambda(n') e(alpha n') ll left((log M)^-1/2 + (log N)^-1/700 right) M N. Since M geqslant H_0 and log N geqslant (log H)^2, this upper bound is ll (log H)^-c' where c' = 1/350. Putting everything together, we conclude that T_M ll left(varepsilon +fraccurlyLexp4J\, V_[M]varepsilon^4 (log M )^4 (log H)^c' right) N. We choose varepsilon = V^J (log M )^-1 (log H)^-c'/5 and deduce the claimed bound crefeq:dyadicsufficient.

Since |b_i| leqslant K H for all iin sintervalK, we have sum_substackboldsymboldin D_\!K sum_substacknin I_N\\ exists i,\, n+b_i notin I_N \!\!1 ll (2H)^K cdot K H ll N. Given boldsymboldin D_\!K and a subset X of Ptimes sintervalK, write I_N(X, boldsymbold) for the set of all nin I_N such that, for all (p, i)in Ptimes sintervalK, pmid n+b_i iff (p,i)in X. Summing over all possibilities for X, the expression crefeq:traceexpressionX becomes Tr big((Ad_G)^Kbig) = sum_substackboldsymboldin D_\!K\, sum_substackXsubset Ptimes sintervalK\, sum_nin I_N(X, boldsymbold)w_boldsymbold(n) \ + \, O(N).
